newsitem.title: JAPAN: Formula change may have caused Japan nuclear fire.
newsitem.headline: Formula change may have caused Japan nuclear fire.

text.p: A change in the chemical mix used for reprocessing nuclear waste may have triggered Japan's worst-ever nuclear accident last month, the government's Science and Technology Agency said on Friday.

The March 11 accident at Japan's only plant to reprocess nuclear waste exposed 37 workers to low-level radiation. The state-owned company that runs the plant later admitted that it covered up some aspects of what happened and lied in its official report.

An agency official said the cause of the accident at the facility in Tokaimura, 160 km (100 miles) northeast of Tokyo, could have been due to a change to standard procedures within the bituminisation facility, an agency official said.

Five days before the accident occurred, the Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corp (PNC), operator of the plant, reduced the amount of low-level irradiated liquid waste supplied to the extruder by about 20 percent compared with normal levels, the agency official said.
The extruder mixes irradiated liquid waste with asphalt for storage in drums.
Chemicals such as nitrate and sodium hydroxide which are found in the irradiated liquid waste may have reacted abnormally under the different conditions, the official said.
A spokesman for PNC, which carries out research and operates nuclear power plants, said the change was made for experimental purposes.
The Science and Technology Agency filed a criminal complaint against PNC after the firm admitted earlier this month it had falsified its report on the explosion and fire at the facility.

The PNC said it had incorrectly stated in the report that staff had visually confirmed that a fire at the facility had been extinguished. No staff members had confirmed this and the fire later flared up causing the explosion.
Officials later admitted that they had forced workers to lie about what had happened.
The PNC has had a string of troubles in recent years. The latest accident has brought calls from senior political leaders for the dismantling of the company.

The company's problems have also thrown into doubt Japan's ambitious plans to rely increasingly on nuclear power. With few natural energy resources, Japan is already heavily dependent on nuclear plants to power its industrial base.
